1.title: The 1929 Crash and the Great Depression
1.before: The late-1920s boom was powered by margin buying: loans to brokers for stock purchases had ballooned, and call-money rates ran far above other rates. Herbert Hoover took office in March 1929. The Fed, worried about speculation, raised the New York discount rate to 6% in August 1929. Congress was debating a major tariff increase (what became Smoot-Hawley). Banks were mostly small, with no federal deposit insurance. Abroad, the world was on the gold standard, and the Bank of England raised rates in September 1929 after the Hatry fraud collapsed in London.
1.trigger: Prices slipped through September, then broke on Black Thursday (Oct 24) and on Black Monday and Tuesday (Oct 28-29), when the Dow fell about 13% and 12%. Margin calls forced selling into a falling market.
1.after: Hindsight: a 1930 rally failed, then waves of bank failures (1930-33), the Smoot-Hawley tariff (1930), Britain leaving gold (1931) and a Fed rate hike into the panic turned a crash into the Great Depression. The S&P fell about 85% from its peak and did not regain it until 1954. Interpretation: leverage in the market met tight policy and a fragile, uninsured banking system.

2.title: Banking panic of 1932-33
2.before: Stocks had nearly doubled off the July 1932 bottom. The country was three years into the Depression with unemployment near 25%. Franklin Roosevelt beat Hoover in November 1932, and markets worried he would devalue the dollar. States began declaring bank holidays (Nevada in late 1932, Michigan in February 1933), and gold drained from the banking system.
2.trigger: A nationwide run on banks and on gold through February 1933 culminated in Roosevelt closing every bank in the country on March 6, 1933.
2.after: Hindsight: the Emergency Banking Act (March 9) and reopening of sound banks restored confidence; stocks recovered their losses within about two months. Interpretation: this was a banking-system failure, not a valuation problem.

3.title: The 1933 speculative collapse
3.before: After the bank holiday, stocks roughly doubled in a few months on New Deal optimism, the end of the gold standard for domestic purposes, and expected repeal of Prohibition. The National Industrial Recovery Act set up industry codes and price controls.
3.trigger: In mid-July 1933 a speculative blow-off in commodities and 'repeal' stocks reversed sharply as the economy's early rebound faded.
3.after: Hindsight: a short, sharp correction inside a strong recovery; prices regained the peak within a few months.

4.title: 1934-35: Gold devaluation and New Deal uncertainty
4.before: The Gold Reserve Act (January 1934) devalued the dollar to $35 per ounce of gold. The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 created the SEC. Businesses faced uncertainty about NRA codes and new regulation, and the Supreme Court was weighing whether 'gold clauses' in contracts would be honored.
4.trigger: A slow grind lower through 1934 as the recovery stalled and policy uncertainty piled up.
4.after: Hindsight: the Supreme Court's gold-clause rulings (February 1935) removed a major uncertainty, and stocks began a strong two-year rally from March 1935.

5.title: Recession of 1937-38
5.before: The recovery from 1933 was strong and stocks had more than doubled. Worried about inflation and excess bank reserves, the Fed doubled reserve requirements in steps from August 1936 to May 1937, and the Treasury began sterilizing gold inflows. Fiscal policy also tightened as the government aimed to balance the budget and new Social Security payroll taxes began.
5.trigger: Industrial production rolled over from mid-1937, and stocks collapsed in the autumn of 1937.
5.after: Hindsight: real GDP fell about 10% and unemployment jumped back toward 20%, America's third-worst downturn of the century. The S&P fell about 45%. Interpretation: a classic case of tightening monetary and fiscal policy too early in a recovery.

6.title: World War II comes to America (1939-42)
6.before: Europe was sliding toward war: the Munich agreement (September 1938) bought time, but Germany invaded Poland in September 1939. The US economy was recovering from the 1937-38 slump with rates near zero.
6.trigger: The fall of France in May-June 1940 brought the sharpest drop. Pearl Harbor (December 1941) and early Allied defeats in the Pacific pushed stocks to new lows, along with wartime price controls and excess-profits taxes.
6.after: Hindsight: the low came in April 1942, just before the Battle of Midway turned the Pacific war. Stocks then rose steadily through the war.

7.title: Post-war inflation and demobilization (1946-49)
7.before: The war ended in 1945. Economists widely expected a post-war depression as millions of soldiers came home. Wartime price controls (OPA) were being dismantled, and the Fed was pegging Treasury yields at low levels.
7.trigger: Once price controls ended in mid-1946, inflation surged (consumer prices rose about 18% in a year) and a wave of strikes hit. Stocks dropped sharply from August to October 1946.
7.after: Hindsight: the feared depression never came, but inflation, a mild 1948-49 recession, and Truman's surprise 1948 election win kept stocks flat-to-down until mid-1949.

8.title: Korean War shock (1950)
8.before: The economy was booming out of the 1949 recession and stocks were at post-1929 highs.
8.trigger: North Korea invaded South Korea on June 25, 1950. Markets feared a wider war with China and the USSR, plus a return to wartime controls.
8.after: Hindsight: a quick, sharp drop; the market recovered within about two months as war spending boosted the economy.

9.title: 1953: Post-Korea slowdown and the bond squeeze
9.before: Eisenhower took office in January 1953. The 1951 Treasury-Fed Accord had freed the Fed from pegging rates, and in spring 1953 a new long-term Treasury bond and tighter policy pushed yields up sharply. A Korean armistice was approaching, which meant defense cuts.
9.trigger: A spring 1953 squeeze in the bond market and expectations of lower defense spending.
9.after: Hindsight: the Korean armistice came in July 1953 and a mild recession ran from July 1953 to May 1954. The Fed eased quickly and stocks began a powerful bull market.

10.title: Eisenhower's heart attack (1955)
10.before: A strong bull market was in full swing, with the economy booming.
10.trigger: President Eisenhower suffered a heart attack on September 24, 1955. The next trading day the market had its worst one-day drop since 1929, on fears about political leadership.
10.after: Hindsight: a pure sentiment shock. Eisenhower recovered and the market regained its peak within weeks.

11.title: Tight money, Suez and Sputnik (1956-57)
11.before: Inflation was creeping up and the Fed raised the discount rate repeatedly in 1955-57, reaching 3.5% in August 1957. Interest rates hit their highest levels in decades. The Suez Crisis (October-November 1956) rattled markets abroad.
11.trigger: The economy rolled over in mid-1957. The Soviet launch of Sputnik on October 4, 1957 added a jolt of fear about American technological and military standing.
11.after: Hindsight: a sharp recession ran from August 1957 to April 1958. The Fed cut rates quickly and stocks recovered in 1958.

12.title: Steel strike and the 1960 recession
12.before: Long-term Treasury yields had climbed above 4% for the first time since the 1920s, and the Fed kept policy tight. A 116-day national steel strike began in July 1959.
12.trigger: The strike disrupted manufacturing, and the economy weakened into 1960 under tight money. The Nixon-Kennedy election added uncertainty.
12.after: Hindsight: a recession ran from April 1960 to February 1961. Stocks bottomed in October 1960 and rallied after the election.

13.title: The Kennedy Slide (1962)
13.before: Stocks had run up on enthusiasm for growth and electronics companies, with price-to-earnings ratios near their highest since 1929. The economy was healthy and inflation low.
13.trigger: In April 1962 President Kennedy publicly forced US Steel to reverse a price increase, which business saw as hostile. Selling built through May and peaked in a 'flash crash' on May 28, 1962.
13.after: Hindsight: no recession followed. The 28% drop was mainly a valuation reset, and stocks recovered over the next year, helped by the Cuban Missile Crisis passing without war in October 1962.

14.title: Credit crunch of 1966
14.before: Vietnam War escalation plus Great Society spending were overheating the economy, and inflation was rising. The Fed raised the discount rate in December 1965 against the administration's wishes. Long-term Treasury yields pushed toward 5%, levels not seen in decades.
14.trigger: By summer 1966, rate ceilings on bank deposits (Regulation Q) caused money to flee savings institutions, mortgage lending dried up, and the municipal bond market was disrupted. Banks scrambled for funds in what became known as the credit crunch of 1966.
14.after: Hindsight: the Fed eased in late 1966, no recession followed, and stocks recovered by 1967. Interpretation: an early example of rising long rates plus credit plumbing stress hitting stocks without a recession; one of the closer analogs to a '10-year near 5%' world.

15.title: Sterling devaluation and the gold crisis (1967-68)
15.before: Inflation and deficits were building. Britain devalued the pound in November 1967, putting pressure on the dollar's link to gold.
15.trigger: The Tet Offensive (January 1968) shook confidence about Vietnam, and a run on gold forced the creation of a two-tier gold market in March 1968.
15.after: Hindsight: President Johnson announced he would not seek re-election at the end of March 1968, a tax surcharge was enacted, and stocks rallied to new highs by late 1968.

16.title: End of the go-go years (1968-70)
16.before: Late-1960s markets were dominated by speculative 'go-go' funds, conglomerates and glamour stocks. Inflation ran near 5-6%, and the Fed under Martin tightened hard in 1969, pushing short rates near 9%. Wall Street was struggling with a back-office 'paperwork crisis' that sank some brokerages.
16.trigger: Tight money slowed the economy into a recession starting December 1969. In spring 1970, the US incursion into Cambodia and the Kent State shootings (May 4) hit sentiment.
16.after: Hindsight: stocks bottomed in May 1970. Weeks later Penn Central, then the largest bankruptcy in US history, defaulted on its commercial paper and the Fed had to backstop that market. The recession ended in November 1970.

17.title: The Nixon shock (1971)
17.before: Inflation remained stubborn and the dollar was under pressure as other countries converted dollars to gold.
17.trigger: On August 15, 1971, Nixon closed the gold window, imposed a wage-price freeze and added a 10% import surcharge. Stocks jumped, then faded through the autumn on uncertainty about controls and the dollar.
17.after: Hindsight: stocks bottomed in November 1971 and rallied into the 'Nifty Fifty' peak of early 1973.

18.title: 1973-74: Nifty Fifty, oil embargo and Watergate
18.before: Big 'one-decision' growth stocks (the Nifty Fifty) traded at very high valuations. The Bretton Woods system had collapsed and currencies began floating in March 1973. Inflation was accelerating and the Fed pushed short rates above 10%. The Watergate scandal was growing.
18.trigger: The Arab oil embargo in October 1973 quadrupled oil prices. Inflation jumped into double digits, and banking scares followed (Franklin National and Germany's Herstatt Bank in 1974). Nixon resigned in August 1974.
18.after: Hindsight: a severe recession ran from November 1973 to March 1975, and the S&P fell about 48%; in real terms it was one of the worst bear markets ever. It took until 1980 to regain the nominal peak.

19.title: New York City fiscal crisis (1975)
19.before: Stocks had rallied hard off the late-1974 low as the recession ended, but inflation stayed high.
19.trigger: New York City was shut out of credit markets and edged toward default in mid-1975, raising fears about municipal finance and the banks holding city debt.
19.after: Hindsight: a short correction; a state and federal rescue avoided default and the market recovered by early 1976.

20.title: Inflation and the falling dollar (1976-78)
20.before: Inflation, which had eased after 1974, began rising again. The new Carter administration pursued stimulus, and the dollar started sliding against other currencies.
20.trigger: A long grind lower through 1977 as the dollar fell sharply and the Fed raised rates. A long coal strike in winter 1977-78 added to the gloom.
20.after: Hindsight: no recession yet; stocks bottomed in March 1978. Inflation kept accelerating toward the double-digit peak of 1979-80.

21.title: The Volcker shock (October 1979)
21.before: Inflation was above 10% and the second oil shock was underway after the Iranian revolution. Paul Volcker became Fed chair in August 1979.
21.trigger: On Saturday, October 6, 1979, the Fed announced it would target the money supply and let interest rates rise as needed. Rates jumped and stocks fell; the Iran hostage crisis began November 4.
21.after: Hindsight: a quick correction, but it marked the start of the most aggressive anti-inflation campaign in Fed history.

22.title: Credit controls and Silver Thursday (1980)
22.before: Inflation ran near 14% and the prime rate approached 20%. The economy entered recession in January 1980, though that wasn't announced until June.
22.trigger: On March 14, 1980 the Carter administration imposed consumer credit controls. The Hunt brothers' attempt to corner silver collapsed on 'Silver Thursday,' March 27, threatening their brokers and banks.
22.after: Hindsight: the low came on Silver Thursday itself. Credit controls were lifted that summer, the brief recession ended in July 1980, and stocks rallied to new highs.

23.title: The Volcker recession (1980-82)
23.before: Ronald Reagan won the November 1980 election. Volcker kept short-term rates around 19-20%, and real interest rates were at record highs. Long-term Treasury yields were above 13%.
23.trigger: Tight money pushed the economy into a deep recession from July 1981; unemployment climbed toward 11%. In summer 1982 Penn Square Bank failed and Mexico announced it could not pay its debts.
23.after: Hindsight: the Fed eased in the summer of 1982, stocks bottomed on August 12, 1982, and an 18-year bull market began. The recession ended in November 1982 and inflation fell below 5%.

24.title: Rates rise again and Continental Illinois (1983-84)
24.before: The economy was booming out of the recession, but large federal deficits and a strong recovery pushed rates back up; the Fed raised the fed funds rate toward 11.5% in 1984. The dollar was very strong.
24.trigger: Rising rates weighed on stocks, and in May 1984 Continental Illinois, then the seventh-largest US bank, suffered a run and needed a government rescue.
24.after: Hindsight: no recession. The Fed eased later in 1984 and stocks began a big rally that ran into 1987.

25.title: Black Monday (1987)
25.before: Stocks were up about 40% for the year by August 1987. Meanwhile bond yields had climbed from about 7% to above 10% in 1987, the dollar was weak, the trade deficit was large, and there was friction between the US and Germany over currencies. Many big investors used 'portfolio insurance' that sold futures automatically as prices fell.
25.trigger: In mid-October, a bad trade-deficit number, comments about letting the dollar fall, and a House proposal to tax takeover financing hit stocks. On Monday, October 19, the S&P fell about 20% in a single day as portfolio-insurance selling overwhelmed buyers.
25.after: Hindsight: the Fed under Greenspan promised liquidity the next morning, no recession followed, and the S&P regained its peak in mid-1989. Interpretation: rapidly rising bond yields against stretched stock valuations, plus mechanical selling, produced a crash without an economic cause. A key analog for a rising-yields world.

26.title: UAL deal collapse and the junk-bond bust (1989-90)
26.before: The late-1980s leveraged buyout boom was financed with junk bonds. The savings and loan crisis was being cleaned up through the new Resolution Trust Corporation.
26.trigger: On Friday, October 13, 1989, financing for the UAL (United Airlines) buyout collapsed, sparking a sharp drop. The junk-bond market kept weakening into early 1990, and Drexel Burnham Lambert filed for bankruptcy in February 1990.
26.after: Hindsight: a modest correction; stocks recovered by mid-1990 before the Gulf War shock.

27.title: Gulf War and the 1990-91 recession
27.before: Banks were weighed down by bad commercial real-estate loans and the savings and loan cleanup, and regulators were tightening capital rules, which made credit harder to get.
27.trigger: Iraq invaded Kuwait on August 2, 1990 and oil prices roughly doubled.
27.after: Hindsight: a recession had quietly started in July 1990 (announced only in April 1991). Stocks bottomed in October 1990 and rallied as the war approached and the Fed cut rates.

28.title: Asian financial crisis (1997)
28.before: The US economy was strong and stocks were rising fast. In Asia, Thailand devalued the baht in July 1997, and the crisis spread to Indonesia, Malaysia and South Korea.
28.trigger: Hong Kong's market crashed on October 23, 1997. On October 27 the Dow fell over 7% and new exchange 'circuit breakers' halted trading for the first time.
28.after: Hindsight: a quick drop; US stocks recovered within weeks as the domestic economy stayed strong.

29.title: Russia default and LTCM (1998)
29.before: Asia was still in crisis and emerging markets were fragile. US stocks were richly valued.
29.trigger: Russia defaulted on its debt and devalued the ruble on August 17, 1998. Credit spreads exploded and Long-Term Capital Management, a huge leveraged hedge fund, neared collapse.
29.after: Hindsight: the New York Fed organized a $3.6 billion private rescue of LTCM in September, and the Fed cut rates three times. Stocks regained their highs by November.

30.title: Fed hikes and Y2K jitters (1999)
30.before: The dot-com boom was in full swing and valuations were at record highs (CAPE above 40). The Fed began raising rates in June 1999 to cool the economy.
30.trigger: Rising Treasury yields and worries about Y2K computer problems led to a summer-autumn correction.
30.after: Hindsight: a short correction; the final leg of the tech bubble took stocks to their peak in March 2000.

31.title: Dot-com bust, 9/11 and accounting scandals (2000-02)
31.before: The S&P traded at a record CAPE of about 44. Telecom and internet companies were spending heavily on infrastructure, often financed with debt and vendor financing from equipment makers like Lucent and Nortel. The Fed raised rates to 6.5% by May 2000.
31.trigger: The Nasdaq peaked on March 10, 2000. Profitless dot-coms ran out of cash, telecom carriers defaulted, and capex collapsed.
31.after: Hindsight: a recession ran from March to November 2001, 9/11 hit markets, and accounting frauds at Enron (2001) and WorldCom (2002) destroyed trust. The S&P fell about 49% and the Nasdaq about 78%; equipment makers that had financed their own customers were crushed. Interpretation: the closest historical match to an AI capex boom financed with debt and vendor deals.

32.title: Global Financial Crisis (2007-09)
32.before: US home prices had peaked in 2006 and were starting to fall. Subprime lender New Century went bankrupt in April 2007, two Bear Stearns hedge funds collapsed in June, and in August BNP Paribas froze funds it couldn't value. The Fed began cutting rates in September 2007, and stocks hit a record high in October.
32.trigger: Mortgage losses spread through the banking system. Bear Stearns was rescued in March 2008, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac were seized in early September, and Lehman Brothers failed on September 15, 2008, followed by the AIG rescue and the TARP bank bailout.
32.after: Hindsight: the recession ran from December 2007 to June 2009 (announced only in December 2008). The S&P fell about 57% and bottomed on March 9, 2009, then took about four years to regain its peak.

33.title: European debt crisis and the Flash Crash (2010)
33.before: The economy was in an early, fragile recovery with rates near zero. Greece's budget problems were coming to light.
33.trigger: Greece needed a bailout in May 2010 and fears spread across Europe. On May 6, 2010 a 'flash crash' briefly erased about $1 trillion in minutes.
33.after: Hindsight: worries about a double-dip recession faded once the Fed signaled more bond buying (QE2) in August; stocks regained the peak by November.

34.title: US downgrade and the euro crisis (2011)
34.before: The Fed's QE2 bond buying ended in June 2011. A Washington standoff over raising the debt ceiling dragged into the summer, and the euro crisis was spreading to Italy and Spain.
34.trigger: Congress raised the debt ceiling at the last minute, but on August 5, 2011 S&P downgraded the US credit rating from AAA. Stocks plunged.
34.after: Hindsight: no recession; the Fed's 'Operation Twist' and European action (the ECB's 2012 pledge) eventually calmed markets. The S&P regained its peak in early 2012.

35.title: China devaluation and the oil-credit bust (2015-16)
35.before: Oil had collapsed from above $100 to around $60, crushing heavily indebted shale drillers. The strong dollar hurt earnings and the Fed was preparing its first rate hike in nine years.
35.trigger: China unexpectedly devalued the yuan on August 11, 2015, and its stock market crashed. Oil kept falling toward $26, junk-bond spreads in the energy sector blew out, and the Fed hiked in December 2015.
35.after: Hindsight: a 'manufacturing and energy recession' but no overall US recession. The Fed slowed its planned hikes, oil rebounded, and stocks recovered by mid-2016. Interpretation: a modern case of credit stress concentrated in one debt-funded, capex-heavy sector.

36.title: Volmageddon (February 2018)
36.before: Stocks had climbed steadily with very low volatility after the 2017 tax-cut law, and many investors were betting volatility would stay low.
36.trigger: A strong wage-growth report on February 2, 2018 pushed bond yields up. On February 5 volatility spiked and several 'short volatility' products collapsed, forcing more selling.
36.after: Hindsight: a fast 10% correction with no economic damage; the market regained its high by August.

37.title: Fed tightening and the trade war (late 2018)
37.before: The Fed was raising rates every quarter and shrinking its balance sheet on 'autopilot'. The 10-year yield rose above 3.2%. Tariffs between the US and China were escalating.
37.trigger: Fed Chair Powell said in early October that rates were 'a long way from neutral.' Tech stocks sold off, trade tensions rose, the Fed hiked again in December, and a government shutdown began December 22.
37.after: Hindsight: stocks bottomed on Christmas Eve 2018. In January 2019 the Fed signaled a pause and later cut rates; the market recovered by April 2019.

38.title: COVID-19 crash (2020)
38.before: Stocks were at record highs with unemployment near 3.5%. A new virus was spreading in China in January 2020.
38.trigger: COVID-19 spread worldwide in late February and March 2020. Economies locked down, oil prices collapsed in a Saudi-Russia price war, and even the Treasury market seized up.
38.after: Hindsight: the fastest bear market on record (about 34% in a month). The Fed cut to zero and launched unlimited bond buying on March 23, the very day of the low, and Congress passed the CARES Act. The S&P regained its peak by August 2020. The recession lasted just two months.

39.title: Inflation and the Fed's fastest hikes since the 1980s (2022)
39.before: Inflation was running near 7% and rising, while the Fed's rate was still near zero. Speculative assets (unprofitable tech, crypto, meme stocks) had soared. Valuations were near record highs (CAPE about 37).
39.trigger: The Fed began hiking in March 2022 and moved in 0.75-point steps by summer. Russia invaded Ukraine on February 24, sending energy prices up. The 10-year yield rose from about 1.5% to over 4%, and the UK had a pension-driven bond crisis in September.
39.after: Hindsight: no recession was declared. Stocks bottomed in October 2022 as inflation peaked; the S&P regained its high in January 2024, led by AI-related stocks. Speculative tech fell far more than the index.

40.title: The 2023 bond-yield scare
40.before: The Fed had raised rates to 5.25-5.5% and signaled 'higher for longer.' Regional banks had failed in March 2023 (Silicon Valley Bank). AI enthusiasm had driven big tech stocks up sharply.
40.trigger: Fitch downgraded the US credit rating on August 1, 2023, and the Treasury announced larger borrowing. Long-term yields surged, with the 10-year touching 5% in mid-October for the first time since 2007. War broke out between Israel and Hamas on October 7.
40.after: Hindsight: stocks bottomed on October 27, 2023. When the Treasury shifted borrowing toward short-term bills and the Fed held rates steady in early November, yields fell and stocks rallied to new highs. Interpretation: a direct precedent for a '10-year at 5%' scare that resolved without a recession.

41.title: Tariff shock (2025)
41.before: Stocks were at record highs, led by AI stocks. In late January 2025, China's DeepSeek released a cheap, capable AI model, and Nvidia fell about 17% in one day, the first big scare about AI spending. The new administration was raising tariffs.
41.trigger: On April 2, 2025, the administration announced sweeping 'reciprocal' tariffs. Stocks fell more than 10% in two days, and in a rare twist Treasury yields jumped at the same time, so bonds didn't cushion the fall.
41.after: Hindsight: on April 9 most new tariffs were paused for 90 days, triggering one of the biggest one-day rallies ever. The S&P regained its high by late June 2025. No recession was declared.
